questions.q: When you launch a cloud VM (like an AWS EC2 instance), what are you actually getting?
options: Brand-new physical hardware racked specifically for you
A virtual machine carved out of a physical server that was already running, via a hypervisor that was already there
A dedicated physical server with no other customers on it, by default
A container, not a virtual machine
questions.explain: Cloud providers run massive fleets of hypervisor hosts; launching a VM carves a new guest out of already-running physical capacity.

options: A container runtime used instead of a hypervisor
AWS's lightweight hypervisor platform combined with dedicated Nitro Cards that offload networking, storage, and security
A programming language used to write AWS Lambda functions
A type of physical cable used in AWS datacenters
questions.explain: AWS Nitro combines a lightweight KVM-based hypervisor with dedicated offload hardware, freeing more of the physical server's CPU for customer VMs.

questions.q: Why can a cloud provider launch a new VM in seconds instead of the hours or days it takes to provision a physical server?
options: Cloud VMs don't actually require any physical hardware at all
The hypervisor and physical capacity are already running; launching a VM is just a software operation starting a new guest from a template
Cloud providers only sell VMs that were pre-built years in advance
Cloud VMs skip the need for a hypervisor entirely
questions.explain: Because the hypervisor and physical server are already running 24/7, an API call to launch an instance is just a fast software request to start a new VM — no racking or cabling needed.

questions.q: What is multi-tenancy in the context of cloud computing?
options: Each customer gets a dedicated physical server with no sharing at all
Multiple customers' VMs running safely on the same shared physical hardware, isolated by the hypervisor
A single customer renting multiple cloud accounts
A security vulnerability unique to public clouds
questions.explain: Multi-tenancy means different customers' VMs can share the same physical server, with the hypervisor enforcing strict isolation between them.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what does the shared responsibility model divide?
options: Which customer pays for which portion of the cloud bill
Security duties: the provider secures the hypervisor and physical hardware, while the customer secures the guest OS, apps, and data
Which programming language each customer must use
How many regions a customer's account can access
questions.explain: The shared responsibility model draws the line at the hypervisor: the provider secures that layer and the hardware beneath it, while the customer is responsible for everything inside their own VM and up.
